First listed: 2026-03-13 | Evaluation cutoff: 2026-11-10

## Source versions

- [YouTube: The Iran War Crisis: Ex-CIA Analyst Helima Croft on Oil Shock & Energy Risk | The Weekly Wrap](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VWMaZ8NPOxE) - 2026-03-13
- [Substack: The Iran War Crisis: Ex-CIA Analyst Helima Croft on Oil Shock & Energy Risk | The Weekly Wrap](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/the-iran-war-crisis-ex-cia-analyst-863) - 2026-03-13

Earliest listed publication among matched versions, not proof of an unedited contemporaneous archive. Claim timestamps refer to the reviewed version.

## Summary

Eisman frames the Iran war as a dominant source of market uncertainty and reiterates Oracle’s funding risk. Guest Helima Croft explains why blocked shipping, limited storage, LNG dependence and vulnerable bypass routes make a prolonged conflict economically damaging. Subsequent physical-market evidence supports her warning about persistent supply stress and alternative-route vulnerability. These are Croft’s forecasts, not Eisman’s. The interview usefully distinguishes military targets from economic normalization, but private-source interpretations of leaders’ intentions and exact war timelines remain unverified. Neither a price move nor a politician’s statement establishes a durable reopening.

Full transcript read. This bounded evidence audit retains unresolved outcomes where matched primary verification is missing; those are not adverse accuracy grades.

- [Oil Market Report, March 2026](https://www.iea.org/reports/oil-market-report-march-2026) (2026-03-12): Hormuz flows fell from about 20 million barrels/day to a trickle; storage constraints drove at least 10 million barrels/day of Gulf production cuts. Members authorized 400 million barrels of reserves. Oil and product shortages, limited bypass capacity and severe price volatility were observed.
- [Oil Market Report, October 2026](https://www.iea.org/reports/oil-market-report-october-2026) (2026-10-14): Observed September inventories were 509 million barrels below end-February; diesel exports remained depressed. Gulf crude flows recovered substantially, but product flows remained below half prewar. Report records September 11 East-West pipeline bombing and heightened Houthi attacks in October. Full-year demand/supply numbers remain forecasts.

### 003. Oracle’s need for external financing makes its balance sheet a continuing concern despite rapid AI-related growth.

**Right** | Steve Eisman | explanation | major

[Source at 2:59-4:11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VWMaZ8NPOxE&t=179s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

Assessment test: Reconcile capex, cash generation, financing, prepayments and customer-provided equipment.

- [Fiscal 2026 second-quarter results](https://investor.oracle.com/investor-news/news-details/2025/Oracle-Announces-Fiscal-Year-2026-Second-Quarter-Financial-Results/default.aspx) (2025-12-10): RPO $523 billion, revenue $16.1 billion. Six-month operating cash flow $10.206 billion versus capex $20.535 billion. Trailing FCF negative $13.181 billion. Current/noncurrent borrowings $8.091/$99.984 billion, previously $7.271/$85.297 billion.
- [Fiscal 2026 third-quarter financial results](https://www.oracle.com/news/announcement/q3fy26-earnings-release-2026-03-10/) (2026-03-10): Revenue $17.2 billion, up 22%; non-GAAP EPS $1.79; RPO $553 billion. Oracle raised $30 billion of bonds and mandatory convertible preferred after announcing up to $50 billion debt/equity financing. Most incremental Q3 AI RPO involved customer prepayments or customer-supplied GPUs.

## Framework and tools

- Eisman distinguishes uncertainty-driven trading from ordinary earnings analysis.
- He asks the guest to explain physical mechanisms and disclose experience-based biases.
- Croft separates military objectives, shipping normalization, storage exhaustion and production restart.
- Scenario duration and alternative-route security matter more than a single oil-price headline.

Tools and charts discussed, not a complete visual inspection:

- Oracle revenue, non-GAAP EPS, RPO and funding plan
- Hormuz daily vessel and oil-flow estimates
- SPR inventories and hypothetical depletion arithmetic
- Regional shut-ins, storage capacity, LNG restart constraints
- Saudi East-West pipeline and Red Sea alternatives

## Source cautions

Steve Eisman narrates the first four minutes and then interviews Helima Croft. Croft supplies most physical-market and geopolitical analysis. Questions, acknowledgments and praise are not treated as Eisman endorsing each guest claim.
- Wrap recorded March 12, interview recorded March 11, upload March 13.
- Opening montage repeats the interview.
- Captions render shale as shell and stockpile as stock power.
- Most geopolitical and energy predictions are Croft’s; Eisman’s questions and brief acknowledgments do not imply adoption.
- Oracle historical quarter/peak chronology is imprecise, while the current report is fiscal Q3 2026.
